hints: Count the valence electrons on nitrogen and hydrogen, then work out how many shared pairs are needed for each hydrogen to gain a duet and nitrogen to gain an octet.
Remember nitrogen in Group 15 starts with five outer electrons, so after forming three bonds think about what is left unshared on nitrogen.
Use electron pair repulsion ideas to decide the shape, three bonding pairs plus one lone pair gives the same family of shapes as an ammonium ion missing one bond.
walkthrough:
Build the electron count**
Think of yourself sitting with N in the middle. N has 5 outer electrons, each H brings 1. That is 8 electrons total to place. Pair each H with N using a shared pair, that uses 3 pairs or 6 electrons. You have 2 electrons left, they must sit on N as a lone pair. Show N electrons as crosses and H electrons as dots, or vice versa, with each bond containing one dot and one cross.

Check the octet**
Look at N now. It has three shared pairs plus one lone pair, that is 8 electrons around N, a full octet. Each H has one shared pair, a full duet. A common slip is to forget the lone pair on N, but without it N would have only 6 electrons.

Name the shape from electron pairs**
You have 4 electron pairs in total but only 3 are bonding. The lone pair repels more strongly and pushes the three N-H bonds down. This gives a trigonal pyramidal shape with bond angle about $107^{\circ}$, like a pyramid with N at the apex.

Final answer: Dot-and-cross shows N central with three N-H bonding pairs and one lone pair on N, giving N an octet.
Shape = trigonal pyramidal.

hints: Recall where electron density lies for a sigma bond relative to the line joining the two nuclei.
Contrast this with a pi bond, think about sideways overlap of p orbitals and where the electron density sits relative to that same line.
walkthrough:
Picture the sigma bond**
Imagine the C nucleus and N nucleus with a straight line between them. A sigma bond is direct end-on overlap along that line. Draw two orbital lobes meeting between the nuclei, with the dots for C and N inside, and shade the overlap region on the axis. That is the strongest part of the triple bond.

Picture the pi bond**
Now think sideways. A pi bond comes from p orbitals overlapping side by side, not end on. Draw the C and N nuclei still on the central line, but draw two separate lobes of electron density, one above the line and one below the line. There is a nodal plane along the nuclei where there is zero pi density.

Final answer: Sigma ($\sigma$): end-on overlap of orbitals with electron density on the C-N internuclear axis between the C and N nuclei.
Pi ($\pi$): sideways overlap of p orbitals with electron density above and below the C-N axis, with nuclei on the axis.

hints: Think about the two words separately, what keeps happening and what stays constant in a closed system.
walkthrough:
Unpack dynamic and equilibrium**
Dynamic tells you the reaction has not stopped, both $\text{CH}_4 + \text{NH}_3 + 1.5\text{O}_2 \rightleftharpoons \text{HCN} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$ directions are still reacting. Equilibrium tells you there is no overall change because the forward rate equals the reverse rate, so all concentrations stay constant in a closed system.
Final answer: Forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate so concentrations remain constant.

hints: Count the total moles of gas on each side of $\text{CH}_4(\text{g}) + \text{NH}_3(\text{g}) + 1.5\text{O}_2(\text{g}) \rightleftharpoons \text{HCN}(\text{g}) + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{g})$.
Recall how Le Chatelier predicts the shift when pressure is increased, toward the side with fewer gas particles.
walkthrough:
Count the gas moles**
Add them up. Left: $1 + 1 + 1.5 = 3.5$ mol gas. Right: $1 + 3 = 4$ mol gas. Increasing pressure squeezes the mixture, so the system wants to reduce the number of particles.

Apply the shift and state the result**
The position of equilibrium moves to the left, toward fewer moles, to oppose the pressure rise. That means less $\text{HCN}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ form and more $\text{CH}_4$, $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{O}_2$ remain. So the yield of products decreases.

Final answer: Yield of $\text{HCN}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ decreases.
Left side has 3.5 mol gas, right side has 4 mol gas, so increased pressure shifts equilibrium to the left to the side with fewer moles of gas.

hints: Recall the standard shape of number of molecules against molecular energy, starting at the origin, rising to a peak then tailing to the right.
Think about where to mark activation energy on the energy axis and how a catalyst changes that value without changing the curve itself.
Link the area under the curve beyond $E_a$ to the fraction of molecules able to react on collision.
walkthrough:
Sketch the distribution correctly**
Draw number of molecules on the y axis and molecular energy on the x axis. Start at the origin because no molecules have zero energy, rise quickly to a peak for the most probable energy, then fall with a long tail to the right because few molecules have very high energy. The total area under the curve is the total number of molecules.

Add the two activation energies**
Mark $E_a$ on the energy axis. The uncatalysed $E_a$ is further right, the catalysed $E_{a(cat)}$ is to its left. The platinum does not change the curve, it gives a new pathway with lower $E_a$. Only molecules with energy to the right of $E_a$ can react.

Explain the rate increase**
With lower $E_a$, a much larger area under the curve lies beyond $E_a$. That means a greater proportion of molecules have energy $\geqslant E_a$ on collision. Therefore the frequency of successful collisions increases and the rate increases, even though the catalyst is not used up.

Final answer: Correct Boltzmann curve starting at origin, rising to maximum then falling asymptotically to energy axis.
Catalyst provides alternative route of lower $E_a$, marked as $E_{a(cat)}$ to left of $E_{a(uncat)}$.
Greater proportion of molecules have $E \geqslant E_a$, so more frequent successful collisions and increased rate.

hints: Think about the type of reagent $\text{CN}^{-}$ is and the type of compound propanone is, addition across which bond occurs.
walkthrough:
Recognise the pattern**
Propanone, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$, is a ketone with a polar $\text{C=O}$ bond. $\text{CN}^{-}$ is a nucleophile with a lone pair that loves the $\delta+$ carbon. When a nucleophile adds across a carbonyl with no leaving group lost, the family name is nucleophilic addition.
Final answer: Nucleophilic addition.

hints: Start by labelling the polarity of the carbonyl bond in propanone, which atom is delta positive and which is delta negative.
Think about where the lone pair on $\text{CN}^{-}$ attacks and what happens to the pi electrons of the $\text{C=O}$ bond.
Draw the charge and structure of the intermediate formed after $\text{CN}^{-}$ has bonded to carbon.
Consider how that negatively charged oxygen intermediate is converted to a neutral OH group, and what small species provides the proton.
Assemble the final product structure, checking that carbon has four bonds and the new groups are $\text{CN}$ and $\text{OH}$ on the same carbon.
walkthrough:
Show why carbon is attacked**
Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so the carbonyl is polarised $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ and $\text{O}^{\delta-}$. Mark those partial charges on $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$. That $\delta+$ carbon is the electrophilic centre that the nucleophile seeks.

Make the first C-C bond**
Take a curly arrow starting on the lone pair of $\text{CN}^{-}$ and pointing to the $\text{C}^{\delta+}$. At the same time, take a second curly arrow from the $\text{C=O}$ double bond up onto O. The pi bond breaks heterolytically, both electrons go to O. This is the key addition step.

Draw the intermediate**
You now have $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}(\text{CN})\text{O}^{-}$. Carbon is bonded to two $\text{CH}_3$ groups, one $\text{CN}$ and one $\text{O}^{-}$. Oxygen carries a full negative charge with three lone pairs. This alkoxide ion is the intermediate in the first box.

Protonate the alkoxide**
The $\text{O}^{-}$ is strongly basic. It removes $\text{H}^{+}$ from $\text{HCN}$ (or $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ trace). Draw a curly arrow from an $\text{O}^{-}$ lone pair to the $\text{H}^{+}$. This regenerates $\text{CN}^{-}$ and forms an O-H bond.

Give the cyanohydrin product**
The final neutral product is $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}(\text{OH})(\text{CN})$, 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile. Check it: central C has four single bonds, to two $\text{CH}_3$, one OH and one CN. Include all lone pairs on O and N if you draw them fully.

Final answer: Dipole shown as $\text{C}^{\delta+}$-$\text{O}^{\delta-}$ on $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C=O}$.
Curly arrow from lone pair on $\text{CN}^{-}$ to $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ and curly arrow from $\text{C=O}$ to O.
Intermediate: $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}(\text{CN})\text{O}^{-}$.
Curly arrow from $\text{O}^{-}$ lone pair to $\text{H}^{+}$ of $\text{HCN}$.
Product: $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}(\text{OH})\text{CN}$, 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile.
